model.label: Tax-funded regional health service: since 2023, 21 well-being services counties plus Helsinki, financed from the state budget, run health and social care with capped user fees; national health insurance (Kela), funded by state and payroll contributions, reimburses medicines and part of private care; employers provide occupational health care

overview.statement: Since January 2023 Finland's health system has been organised by 21 well-being services counties, the City of Helsinki and the HUS group (the former Helsinki and Uusimaa hospital district); the counties are run by elected councils and paid for out of the state budget.

locator.section: How is the health system organized?

overview.statement: The counties organise primary and secondary health care together with social and rescue services, and set and collect user fees; each belongs to one of five collaborative areas organised around the five university hospitals.

locator.section: How is the health system organized?

overview.statement: Every resident is entitled to publicly funded health services, although in practice access differs with employment status, legal residence and ability to pay.

Primary care runs through three overlapping channels: county health centres, the occupational health care scheme (which relies heavily on contracted private providers) and private providers serving patients directly; higher-education students have their own Student Health Service.
Employers must arrange preventive occupational health care for their employees, and most also buy outpatient medical care for them.

locator.section: How is the health system organized?

overview.statement: The Ministry of Social Affairs and Health prepares health and social care legislation and steers the system, the Ministry of Finance oversees the counties' budgets, borrowing and audits, and the Finnish Institute for Health and Welfare (THL) supplies expertise and, since 2023, evaluates the counties' performance.

locator.section: How is the health system organized?

overview.statement: Community pharmacies are owned by pharmacists; in 2024 there were 639 main pharmacies and 188 subsidiary pharmacies, more than 800 in all.

financing.statement: Before the reform, municipalities paid for health care mainly from local taxes, topped up by state grants and user fees; now central government allocates funds to each county according to population size, demographic make-up and projected service needs, consolidating public financing into what the profile calls a single-payer model.

locator.section: Box 1. Funding is now channelled through the national budget

financing.statement: The counties are funded by central government through a formula: about 80% of the money is allocated by a coefficient for health and social care needs, the rest per capita or by other factors such as bilingualism, foreign languages and population density, and a small share comes from co-payments and sales.

locator.section: How much is spent on health services?

financing.statement: The national health insurance (NHI) scheme is financed by the state, employers, employees and the self-employed through payroll contributions, and it reimburses outpatient prescription medicines, part of the cost of private care, and travel to care.

locator.section: How much is spent on health services?

financing.statement: NHI has two parts. Earned-income insurance pays sickness and parental allowances, rehabilitation allowances and employers' compensation for occupational health services, and is funded mainly by an employer contribution and by a daily-allowance contribution from employees and the self-employed.

When earned-income insurance funding changed at the start of 2025, the employers' NHI contribution covered 68% of its expenditure (excluding family-leave compensation, the extra contribution from the self-employed and the state's share) and the daily-allowance contribution 32%.

Medical care insurance, the NHI part that pays reimbursements for medicines, doctors' and dentists' fees, tests, treatment and travel, has since 2025 been funded 51.4% by the state and 48.6% by the insured.

All insured people, including employees, the self-employed, pensioners and other benefit recipients, pay a medical care contribution on taxable income subject to local government tax; by rule, benefit recipients' rate is 0.39 percentage points above that of wage earners and the self-employed.

In 2026 employers pay a health insurance contribution of 1.91% (1.87% in 2025); on wage income, insured people pay a health care contribution of 1.10% (1.06% in 2025) and a daily allowance contribution of 0.88%, which is zero for annual income below EUR 17,255.

Employers can claim compensation from Kela for occupational health care and medical care costs, typically about half of the calculated maximum costs; providing GP-level medical care is voluntary for employers.
The Finnish Student Health Service is funded 23% by the student healthcare fee and 77% by the state.

In 2023 public sources paid 81% of current health spending, the highest share in two decades; out-of-pocket payments made up 14%, down from a peak of 19% in 2016 and below the EU average of 16%, and voluntary health insurance 5%, on a par with the EU.
The 2025 country profile's spending and financing-share figures for 2023 come from the OECD Data Explorer health accounts dataset (DF_SHA).
In 2021 the state accounted for 67% of current health expenditure, the national health insurance scheme for 13% and private sources for 20%.
About a fifth of the population holds voluntary private health insurance, which covers out-of-pocket payments for public and private services and outpatient medicines.

A 2023 study using one Finnish insurance company's nationwide register data found that local take-up of voluntary health insurance was explained more by sociodemographics than by the supply of care: it was higher where employment, income and education were higher and where private clinics were closer, and was not associated with fees and co-payments.

covered.statement: The statutory benefit package covers primary and specialist care, inpatient services and mental health care, but coverage is narrower for outpatient and rehabilitative services delivered outside hospitals.

Most employed people get outpatient care through occupational health schemes that are free at the point of use and usually faster, though what is covered varies by employer; pensioners, children, the unemployed and the self-employed rely more on public services, which can be slower and carry user charges.

Where public coverage should stop has been debated recently for fertility treatment for single women and female couples, vasectomies, and very costly therapies for cancer and inherited diseases; most gynaecology, eye care and adult dentistry is delivered privately.

locator.section: Box 2 What are the key gaps in coverage?

covered.statement: Who decides what is covered: outpatient medicine prices are set by the Pharmaceuticals Pricing Board and Kela on the basis of health technology assessments by the Finnish Medicines Agency, while hospital medicines are assessed for clinical value by the Council for Choices in Healthcare in Finland.
Coverage for undocumented migrants was extended to non-emergency care in 2023; as of the 2024 summary, the government was considering withdrawing that extension.

cost_sharing.statement: Client fees went up in January 2025, by 22.5% for primary care and 45% for specialist care, while the 2025 annual ceilings stayed the same: EUR 762 (services), EUR 633 (medicines) and EUR 300 (travel), EUR 1,695 combined.
In 2026 the annual ceiling on client fees for public health care is EUR 815, and patients must keep track themselves of how much they have paid towards it.

locator.section: Client fees in public health care

cost_sharing.statement: Outpatient prescription medicines are reimbursed in three tiers, from 40% to 100% depending on the condition and the medicine's assessed therapeutic value, after an annual deductible of EUR 70 (2025); even fully reimbursed medicines carry a fixed co-payment, and once out-of-pocket medicine spending reaches EUR 633.17 a year only a small co-payment remains.
Once the annual limit on medicine costs is passed, patients pay only a EUR 2.50 deductible for covered prescription medicines.

locator.section: Kela, the Social Insurance Institution of Finland

cost_sharing.statement: A 2021 change to user fees lowered annual caps, exempted some groups (such as children) and services (such as nurse visits and psychiatric treatment in primary care) and let people on very low incomes apply for income assistance, yet the 2024 summary still judges financial protection to be limited.
Patients can apply to have public health and social care client fees reduced or waived, and under section 11 of the Act on Client Fees this takes precedence over paying social assistance.

locator.section: Client fees in public health care

cost_sharing.statement: From 1 January 2024 Kela's reimbursement for an appointment with a doctor in private practice, general practitioner or specialist, rose from EUR 8 to EUR 30 (EUR 25 for a remote consultation).

Kela does not reimburse laboratory tests, physiotherapy or other investigations and treatments that a private doctor orders, unless the orders come from a psychiatrist, a dentist or an oral and maxillofacial surgeon.
Occupational health services are free at the point of use, while publicly financed services carry high user charges, with exemptions for some groups and services.

financial_hardship.statement: Unpaid client fees for public health care are classed as directly enforceable debts, and the collection cost that can be charged on such a debt is capped at EUR 51 however hard it is to collect.

locator.section: Debt collection of public health care client fees

financial_hardship.statement: People whose income is garnished can apply to have the garnishment restricted because of large medical expenses.
Kela offers low-income people a medicine cost credit to help them pay up to the annual ceiling on out-of-pocket costs for reimbursed prescription medicines.

locator.section: Kela, the Social Insurance Institution of Finland

financial_hardship.statement: Maximum co-payments for municipal health care were raised substantially in 2015 and 2016; in 2018 there were about 430,000 debt recovery proceedings over unpaid municipal social and health care user charges, up from 180,000 in 2012.
Although cost-containment measures and tight regulation hold spending down, high co-payments for medicines contribute significantly to catastrophic health spending.

additional_care.statement: Since 2023 dental care has been organised by the counties and is delivered at primary level mainly in health centres, which employ more than half of all dentists.

Patients who use private dentists get roughly 12% of the cost (excluding administrative charges) back from national health insurance; cosmetic procedures and prosthodontics are excluded and orthodontics is reimbursed only in specific cases.

Long-term care is organised by the counties, mainly publicly funded but subject to user charges; because long-term care beds have not kept pace with need, falling especially fast since 2009, residential care has become less available and more of the burden has shifted to families.
A statutory therapy guarantee in force since May 2025 requires that people under 23 get brief psychotherapy or targeted psychosocial support, free of charge, within one month of an assessed need.

Reimbursement policy aligns payment and cost-sharing for telemedicine with in-person visits; reimbursed telemedicine users rose from about 3,300 in 2019 to more than 320,000 in 2022, around 12% of all reimbursed medical fees that year, with limited uptake among people over 75.

By 2023 many counties had set up a digital clinic as the first point of contact for primary care, offering assessments and minor consultations by chat or video; these are now available nationwide and are often run by private vendors.

access.statement: In the 2024 EU-SILC survey, 12.4% of people who needed medical care in Finland reported unmet needs because of cost, distance or waiting times, the second highest rate in the EU after Greece; among people at risk of poverty the figure was 20.9%, against an EU average of 6.0% cited in the profile.

People in the lowest income quintile report unmet health needs at double the rate of those in the highest; the summary links the gap to fragmented primary care, in which employed people often get outpatient care through occupational health and those who can pay use private services with little waiting.
In 2024, according to a 2025 Eurofound e-survey, 9% of Finnish adults reported unmet needs for primary care and 12% for mental health care, among the highest rates in the EU and well up on 2021.
Dental care is a major gap: in 2024, 14.8% of people needing dental care reported unmet needs, more than twice the EU average of 6.3%, and 25.6% among low-income groups against 13.6% across the EU.

Average waits for elective surgery lengthened between 2021 and 2024: from 98 to 169 days for hip replacement, 123 to 216 days for knee replacement and 112 to 146 days for cataract surgery, while waits fell in several neighbouring countries such as Sweden and Denmark.
Employed people have better access to outpatient care through the occupational scheme, which is free at the point of use and often has shorter waits because it buys services from the private sector.
In national population surveys around one third of patients said that high user charges had made it hard to get health services (THL, 2023).

locator.section: Box 2 What are the key gaps in coverage?

access.statement: In the 2022-2023 Healthy Finland Survey of people aged 20-64, 41% of unemployed respondents reported an unmet need for a doctor or nurse, and unemployed people were more likely than employed people to report one (odds ratio 2.31).

A mixed-methods study set in rural North Karelia found, from register data, that all GP consultations rose 1.69-fold from 2017 to 2024 while in-person consultations decreased (a 0.60-fold change), and that a change in definition explained the improvement in waiting-time statistics.

outcomes.statement: Life expectancy at birth reached 82.4 years in 2024, above the EU average but below Iceland, Norway and Sweden.
In 2022 Finland's preventable mortality (166 per 100,000) and treatable mortality (71 per 100,000) were both below the EU averages of 168 and 90, though slightly above other Nordic countries.
Treatable mortality fell by 16.5% between 2012 and 2022.
In the GBD 2019 study, Finland's Healthcare Access and Quality (HAQ) Index score for ages 0-74 was 87.7 (95% uncertainty interval 85.5-89.5) in 2019, 19.1 points higher than in 1990.

locator.table: Table: HAQ Index estimates by location; row values in order: 2019 overall (0-74 years), young (0-14), working (15-64), post-working (65-74), then absolute change 1990-2019 for the same four groups

outcomes.statement: Colorectal cancer screening went fully national in 2022, when 77% of the target population completed screening, one of the highest participation rates in Europe.
Breast cancer screening participation held at 82% in 2023, third highest in the EU after Denmark and Sweden, and cervical screening reached 73%, well above the EU average.

In 2023 avoidable hospital admissions were 115 per 100,000 for asthma and COPD (EU average 158) and 85 per 100,000 for diabetes; congestive heart failure admissions, at 211 per 100,000, were below the EU average of 239 but above other Nordic countries.

In 2022 women aged 65 could expect to live another 21.3 years and men another 18.0, but fewer than half of those years were expected to be healthy (43% for women, 49% for men), close to EU averages but well below other Nordic countries.
The maternal mortality ratio in 2017 was reported as 3 deaths per 100,000 live births in Finland against 19 in the United States.

costs.statement: In 2023 Finland spent EUR 3,996 per person on health (adjusted for purchasing power), equal to 10.5% of GDP and slightly above the EU average of 10.0%.
In 2023, 42% of health spending went to outpatient care, one of the highest shares in the EU, while inpatient care took 20%, down from 25% in 2015.

Long-term care accounted for 21% of total health spending, pharmaceuticals 13% and prevention 5%; administrative spending was under 1%, which the profile says places Finland among the most efficient EU countries for health system governance.
Per-person spending on retail pharmaceuticals was EUR 432 in 2023 (purchasing-power adjusted), about 15% below the EU average of EUR 510.
Between 2012 and 2023 hospital spending on medicines rose from EUR 75 to EUR 109 per person, while retail spending barely moved, from EUR 368 to EUR 378.

In their first year the counties ran a combined deficit of EUR 1.7 billion; the Ministry of Finance opened evaluation procedures in three counties, and a temporary amendment lets counties that balance their 2025 budgets defer covering earlier deficits until 2028.

In the first two years of the reform every county ran a deficit, ranging from about EUR 50 million to over EUR 100 million, attributed to rapid cost inflation, renegotiated health workforce pay and possible underreporting of real costs by municipalities.

locator.section: How much is spent on health services?

what_works.statement: Antibiotic consumption dropped from 14.7 to 12.9 defined daily doses per 1,000 people per day between 2019 and 2023, under both the EU average (19.9) and the national target (13.4).
In 2023, WHO Access-group antibiotics made up 74% of national antibiotic consumption, above the complementary target of at least 65%.

Use of online health services is far above the EU average: in 2024, 64% of Finns booked appointments online (EU 40%), 74% accessed their health records (EU 28%) and 79% searched for health information online (EU 58%).

Nurse density, 12.7 per 1,000 people, is among the highest in the EU; specialised primary care nurses can prescribe a limited range of medicines, manage chronic conditions after a doctor's diagnosis and often act as the first point of contact.
No other country had set a legally binding target before Finland to end tobacco and nicotine product use, with 2030 as the deadline.
Daily smoking among adults was 11% in 2022, among the EU's lowest and under half its 2002 level of 23%.
Long-standing cost containment, including generic substitution, reference pricing and extensive e-prescribing, has kept overall pharmaceutical spending fairly stable over the past decade.
Vacant health and social care positions fell from more than 7,300 in early 2023 to around 2,500 by early 2025.
Compared with the other Nordic countries, Finland spent less on health in 2021 yet had a similar, if slightly higher, treatable mortality rate, which has been falling consistently.
Finland's hospital bed numbers fell by 30% and inpatient discharges by 21% between 2017 and 2023, far more than the average reductions across the EU.

problems.statement: Finland had 2.9 practising physicians per 1,000 people in 2023, well below the EU average of 4.3.

Shortages persist in rural and northern regions, where physician density is below 2.0 per 1,000 inhabitants, while unemployment among assistant nurses has risen, a mismatch between workforce supply and demand.

By 2030 more than 20% of staff are expected to retire in over half of the counties, and the sector increasingly relies on part-time and agency staff, which raises costs and can disrupt continuity of care.

In 2023 public schemes paid only 58% of retail pharmaceutical costs, households 39% and voluntary insurance 3%; Finland's out-of-pocket share for medicines is above the EU average but the lowest among the Nordic countries.
Pharmacies act as regional monopolies and earn higher margins on more expensive products, so they have little financial reason to promote lower-cost alternatives.
Reference prices are fixed for three months at a time while manufacturers can change wholesale prices every two weeks, reducing the pressure for price competition.

locator.section: Box 8 Is there waste in pharmaceutical spending?

problems.statement: Parallel funding and delivery systems persist and add to fragmentation and inequity, especially in access to primary care.

In June 2024 the maximum alcohol content of fermented drinks sold in grocery and convenience stores was raised from 5.5% to 8%, prompting concern about wider access to stronger products while alcohol remains the leading cause of preventable deaths.
More than 30% of adults were obese in 2022 on measured height and weight, up from 22% in 2012.

In a 2026 study of primary care access, older patients with chronic needs described growing difficulty navigating an increasingly digital primary care service and getting in-person consultations, and staff reported a stronger need to gatekeep access to GP consultations because of limited resources.
The number of clinical trials in Finland fell from 191 in 2017 to 105 in 2024, a drop of more than 40%.

reforms.statement: The health and social care reform, more than a decade in preparation, was passed by Parliament in summer 2021; counties took full responsibility for services in January 2023 and financing was centralised at national level.

By law a county has three years, counted from the start of the year after its accounts are approved, to make good an accumulated deficit, which means deficits from 2023 have to be eliminated by the end of 2026.

In September 2023 the maximum wait for non-urgent primary care was cut from 3 months to 14 days, and by March 2024, 71% of outpatient appointments took place within that period, up from 58% a year earlier.

In budget negotiations the government agreed to increase Kela reimbursements by EUR 500 million in total over 2024-2027; about EUR 97.5 million was reserved for the following year, EUR 65.3 million of it financed by the state.

In register data (2018-2022) from one major occupational health provider, preventive occupational health services turned from decline to growth after the 2020 reimbursement reform while curative care declined; the authors judge the reform likely contributed, though other factors may also have played a part.
Until recently pharmacies could not substitute biosimilars; phased substitution began in 2024 with enoxaparin and is set to extend to further biologics through 2026.
Since 2023 THL's remit includes annual performance monitoring of the counties, combining guidance, support and evaluation to inform budget negotiations and oversight.
In spring 2024 the government reinstated the 3-month maximum wait for non-urgent primary care as part of a wider austerity package.
A pilot was launched letting people aged 65 and over use national health insurance funds for private care at the same co-payment as at a public health centre.

us_lessons.statement: Based on observing Finnish maternity care (shadowing providers) and a literature review, a 2021 paper describes Finnish perinatal care as a decentralised, community-based primary care network attending to mothers' physical and psychosocial well-being, and suggests it could serve as a template for US efforts to reduce maternal mortality.
